stat_label: Season, set in Display
body: The season nobody beat Arsenal. Thirty-eight league games, twenty-six wins, twelve draws, no defeats. The season a Russian billionaire bought Chelsea and spent more in one summer than the rest of the league together. And the season a club from Porto, coached by a 41-year-old called José Mourinho, won the Champions League.
chart_notes: The season set as one Display numeral across the front cover; no chart.
design_notes: Front (right page) carries only the season numeral and the series line. Back (left) carries the blurb. | Image region is a flat paper field with the numeral in ink; no club crests (licensing) and no photography.
check_before_print: Mourinho's age at the final (41) — born 26 January 1963; confirm before print.

headline: Nobody beat Arsenal. Thirty-eight games, ninety points, eleven clear
stat_label: Arsenal’s league record: won, drawn, lost
body: Six clubs led the Premier League in 2003-04 and the lead changed hands twenty times, most of them before February. After the first of February it never moved again. Arsenal took 45 points from their first nineteen games and 45 from their last nineteen, won 26, drew 12 and lost none, the first unbeaten top-flight season in England since Preston in 1888-89. Behind them Chelsea, rebuilt with Roman Abramovich's money, finished second on 79; Manchester United, top at halfway, fell to third. In Europe the season belonged to clubs nobody had tipped: Porto beat Monaco in the final. This book follows both, month by month.
caption: Cumulative league points after each game, every club. Arsenal and Chelsea highlighted; Manchester United and Liverpool labelled.
chart_encode: x = game number 1–38; y = cumulative points 0–90. One line per club.
chart_highlight: Arsenal in accent, Chelsea in second; Manchester United and Liverpool labelled in muted; the other 16 clubs as 0.5pt muted context lines, unlabelled.
chart_annotate: Game 30, 28 March: “30 unbeaten from the start, a record” (1–1 v Manchester United). | Game 34, 25 April: title won at White Hart Lane, four games left. | Final point labels at the line end: Arsenal 90, Chelsea 79, Man United 75, Liverpool 60.
chart_notes: The chart every later league spread zooms into; keep its scale (0–90) wherever the race returns.
design_notes: Chart region spans the right page (x 6.5–12, y 0–6.75); headline over 2.5 rows at 1.15× Headline. | The 16 context lines are one muted group; no legend, direct labels only at the line ends of the four named clubs. | Draw the two annotation leaders at 0.5pt to the Arsenal line; captions in Caption style.
check_before_print: “First unbeaten top-flight season since Preston 1888–89” is not in our data: confirm wording against a published source.

headline: Chelsea spent two and a half times what the rest of the league did
stat_label: Chelsea’s nine £5m-plus signings, July to 1 September
body: Roman Abramovich bought Chelsea in July 2003, and by the time the transfer window shut the club had signed nine players for £5m or more: Damien Duff, Hernán Crespo, Claude Makélélé, Adrian Mutu, Juan Sebastián Verón and four more. Together they cost £107.8m. Every other Premier League club put together made six signings of that size, for £42.5m, and the biggest of those was Manchester United's £12.24m for an 18-year-old from Sporting called Cristiano Ronaldo. Claudio Ranieri, who had finished fourth the season before, now had two players for most positions. The money bought second place, 79 points, and a Champions League semi-final. It did not buy the title.
caption: Total fees paid for £5m-plus signings, 1 June to 1 September 2003, by Premier League club. Chelsea's bar is split into its nine signings.
source_line: Source: Wikipedia, List of English football transfers summer 2003 (reported fees); £5m-plus moves only.
chart_encode: One horizontal bar per club that made a £5m-plus signing, length = total fee (£m). Chelsea’s bar is segmented by player, largest first.
chart_highlight: Chelsea in accent with player names on the segments (Duff 17.0, Crespo 16.8, Makélélé 16.6, Mutu 15.8, Verón 15.0, Geremi 7.0, Bridge 7.0, Joe Cole 6.6, Glen Johnson 6.0). Other clubs in muted.
chart_annotate: A bracket under the five muted bars: “the other 19 clubs together: £42.5m”.
chart_notes: Order bars by total. Manchester United 18.24 (Ronaldo 12.24, Kléberson 6.0), Blackburn 7.5, Tottenham 6.25, Birmingham 5.5, Liverpool 5.0.
design_notes: Bars run left to right across the gutter in the chart region (x 3.75–12); keep Chelsea’s bar first and full-width so the rest look small at the same scale. | Segment labels inside Chelsea’s bar in Label style, ink on accent at 100% would fail contrast — set them paper on accent. | Stat in Numerals at 54pt in the left column under the headline.

headline: Forty ties to fill sixteen places, and Newcastle lost theirs on penalties
stat_label: Partizan’s shoot-out win at St James’ Park, 19 August
body: The Champions League began on 16 July, a month before the Premier League, with twenty champions of Europe's smaller leagues. By 20 August forty ties had been played and sixteen clubs had won a place in the group stage. Newcastle United, third in England the season before, were one of the casualties. They won 1-0 in Belgrade, lost 1-0 at home to Partizan and went out 4-3 on penalties. Partizan had already needed away goals to beat Djurgården in the previous round. Chelsea, fourth the season before, came through the same round 5-0 against Žilina, and went on to the semi-finals.
caption: Every qualifying tie, July and August 2003, by round. Bars run from first leg to second leg; circles mark ties settled on penalties or away goals.
chart_encode: Three lanes, one per qualifying round (Q1 16–23 Jul, Q2 30 Jul–6 Aug, Q3 12–20 Aug), on a shared date axis 16 July → 20 August. Each tie is a short bar from first-leg to second-leg date; the winner’s name sits at the bar end.
chart_highlight: Newcastle–Partizan in accent; Chelsea–Žilina (5–0 on aggregate) in second. Ties settled on penalties or away goals marked with a small open circle.
chart_annotate: Q3: Partizan 0–1 Newcastle, Newcastle 0–1 Partizan, 4–3 on penalties. | Partizan also needed away goals to get past Djurgården in Q2.
chart_notes: 10 + 14 + 16 = 40 ties; the 16 Q3 winners join the 16 clubs that went straight into the groups.
design_notes: Lanes take the chart band (y 2.75–5.5) across both pages; dates as Label-style ticks every week. | 40 bars is dense; keep winner labels only on Q3 and on the highlighted ties, muted dots elsewhere.
check_before_print: Partizan's away-goals win over Djurgården (3–3) and the shoot-outs are from engsoccerdata's pens column; spot-check against UEFA.

headline: Seventy-two clubs from 48 countries started. By September, 32 were left
stat_label: Clubs that played in the 2003–04 Champions League
body: Seventy-two clubs from 48 countries played in the 2003-04 Champions League. Twenty began in the first qualifying round in mid-July; eighteen more joined in each of the next two rounds; sixteen, the champions and runners-up of the biggest leagues, waited for the group stage. When the groups were drawn there were 32 clubs left, from 15 countries. Both clubs who would reach the final in Gelsenkirchen were among the sixteen that skipped qualifying, but neither had been a favourite: Porto were Portuguese champions and UEFA Cup holders, Monaco had finished second in France. Two of the four semi-finalists, Chelsea and Deportivo, had started in August.
caption: Clubs still in the competition at each stage. Porto and Monaco traced through.
chart_encode: A stepped funnel of vertical bars, one per stage, height = clubs still in (20 → 28 → 32 → 32 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1). Label each step with the stage name and the count.
chart_highlight: Two thin tracks through the steps, Porto in accent and Monaco in second, both entering at the group stage.
chart_annotate: “16 clubs went straight into the groups — both finalists among them.”
chart_notes: Q1 20 clubs, Q2 28 (10 winners + 18 new), Q3 32 (14 + 18), groups 32 (16 + 16), R16 16, QF 8, SF 4, final 2, winner 1.
design_notes: Steps read left to right across the gutter; the group stage step (32) sits on the page break so the qualifying rounds are left, the knockouts right. | Stat 72 in Numerals; count labels in Label style above each step.
check_before_print: Porto as UEFA Cup holders (won May 2003) is outside this season's data; confirm.

headline: Old Trafford held four Loftus Roads
stat_label: Manchester United’s average home league crowd
body: Manchester United averaged 67,641 at Old Trafford, more than four times the 16,342 Fulham drew at Loftus Road, the Queens Park Rangers ground they rented while Craven Cottage was rebuilt. The gap was about more than demand. Newcastle (51,440) and Manchester City (46,834, in their first season at the new City of Manchester Stadium) had the room; Arsenal, the champions, played to 38,079 at Highbury, seventh in the league. Portsmouth, promoted, squeezed 20,108 into Fratton Park. Across the season the Premier League drew about 13.3 million people to 380 games.
caption: Average home league attendance, 2003-04, all twenty clubs, on one scale across both pages.
source_line: Source: worldfootball.net via Wikipedia, 2003–04 FA Premier League.
chart_encode: Twenty horizontal bars, average home attendance, largest first, split across the two pages (1–10 left, 11–20 right) on one shared scale.
chart_highlight: Manchester United in accent, Fulham in second; all others muted.
chart_annotate: Fulham: 16,342 at Loftus Road, the ground they shared while Craven Cottage was rebuilt.
chart_notes: Top: Man United 67,641, Newcastle 51,440, Man City 46,834 (first season at the City of Manchester Stadium). Bottom: Fulham 16,342, Portsmouth 20,108, Blackburn 24,376.
design_notes: Split the ranking at the gutter, not by size; keep the scale identical on both pages so Fulham’s bar is visibly a quarter of United’s. | Value labels at the bar end, tabular numerals.
check_before_print: Fulham's ground share at Loftus Road (2002–04) and City's first season at the new stadium are not in our data; confirm. | The 13.3 million total is avg_attendance × 19 summed over the Wikipedia table (13,297,359).

headline: Until Christmas, first and third were never more than five points apart
stat_label: Biggest gap from first to third, September to December
body: For four months the title was a three-way argument. Between September and the end of December the gap between the leaders and the club in third never grew beyond five points, and the top spot changed hands ten times. Chelsea went top in September after Abramovich's new signings won six of their first nine; Manchester United led at Christmas; Arsenal, who drew 0-0 at Old Trafford in September in a game remembered for the fight at the end, were never out of the top two. The FA fined Arsenal £175,000 for that afternoon, the largest fine it had given a club. Nobody yet thought the season would end without Arsenal losing.
caption: Cumulative points, games 1–19, the top three. The shaded band is the gap from first to third.
source_line: Source: football-data.co.uk; standings by date, 3/1/0, ties on GD then GF.
chart_encode: The intro’s race cropped to 16 August – 31 December (games 1–19); y from 0 to 50 so the three lines separate.
chart_highlight: Arsenal accent, Chelsea second, Manchester United ink at 0.75pt with a direct label (the third series stays un-coloured, per the chart style).
chart_annotate: Shade the band between the top and third line; label its widest point (5 points). | 21 Sep: Manchester United 0–0 Arsenal at Old Trafford (Vieira sent off, Van Nistelrooy missed a late penalty).
chart_notes: The preset draws the whole season; crop to games 1–19 in the layout, not the data.
design_notes: Same line weights and colours as the intro race so the reader recognises the zoom. | The shaded band in draw-grey at 30%, under the lines.
check_before_print: The £175,000 fine is from events.csv (not yet hand-verified).

headline: Liverpool shot more than anyone and finished 30 points behind
stat_label: Liverpool’s league shots, the most of any club
body: Liverpool took 558 league shots in 2003-04, more than any other club and 87 more than Arsenal. They put 300 on target, also the most. They scored 55. Arsenal scored 73 from 273 on target, a goal for every 3.7, against Liverpool's one in 5.5. Only Chelsea converted better. At the other end, Bolton took 533 shots, the second-highest total, and scored 48. Gérard Houllier's side finished fourth, 30 points behind the champions, and he was sacked in May. The numbers are a reminder that shooting a lot and shooting well are different things.
caption: Shots and goals for every club (left), and goals per shot on target (right). Liverpool and Arsenal highlighted.
chart_encode: Left page: x = shots, y = goals, one dot per club. Right page: the same clubs ranked by goals per shot on target (bars).
chart_highlight: Liverpool accent, Arsenal second; the other 18 muted with direct labels for the extremes only (Birmingham fewest shots 328; Bolton and Southampton lowest conversion 0.166).
chart_annotate: Liverpool: 558 shots, 300 on target, 55 goals. Arsenal: 471 shots, 273 on target, 73 goals.
chart_notes: Chelsea had the best goals per shot on target (0.275), Arsenal next (0.267).
design_notes: One visual in two halves per the comparison template; the scatter axes start at zero. | Dot labels in Label style, placed to avoid the leader lines.
check_before_print: Houllier's sacking (24 May 2004) is from events.csv.

headline: The group stage averaged two and a half goals a game. In Monaco one night there were eleven
stat_label: Monaco v Deportivo, 5 November 2003
body: The 96 games of the 2003-04 group stage produced 238 goals, a little under two and a half a game. Seven finished 0-0. Only one went past seven. On 5 November in Monaco, Didier Deschamps' side beat Deportivo La Coruña 8-3, the highest-scoring game the Champions League had seen. Dado Pršo scored four. The odd thing is what happened next: Deportivo, who had beaten Monaco 1-0 in Spain a fortnight earlier, still finished second in the group, knocked out Juventus and the holders Milan, and reached the semi-finals. Monaco went all the way to the final.
caption: All 96 group-stage games, by total goals. Each block is one game.
chart_encode: A histogram of the 96 group games by total goals (0 to 11). Each game is one stacked unit, so the 8–3 stands alone at 11.
chart_highlight: The 8–3 in accent; Juventus 7–0 Olympiacos (7 goals) in second; everything else muted.
chart_annotate: “2.48 goals a game across 96 group matches.” | “Deportivo conceded eight — and reached the semi-finals.”
design_notes: The chart region (x 3.75–12) holds 12 columns of blocks; the gap between 7 and 11 is part of the story, keep the empty columns. | Annotation leader from the 11 column to the second note.
check_before_print: “Highest-scoring game the Champions League had seen”, Pršo’s four goals and Deschamps as Monaco coach are not in our data: confirm against UEFA records.

headline: Dado Pršo’s goals in the 8–3
stat_label: Goals by Dado Pršo, Monaco v Deportivo
caption: Pršo finished the competition with seven goals in 512 minutes, one every 73.
chart_notes: Big number only. Pršo scored 7 Champions League goals in 512 minutes, a goal every 73 minutes (ucl_scorers.csv).

headline: At halfway four points covered the top three. By May it was fifteen
stat_label: Points from first to third, after 19 games and after 38
body: After nineteen games, half a season, Manchester United were top on 46 points, one ahead of Arsenal and four ahead of Chelsea. It was the closest the top three would be all year. Over the second half Arsenal took exactly what they had taken in the first, 45 points, Chelsea took 37 and United 29. By May the gap from first to third was fifteen points. Further down, the table moved less than it felt: Leeds and Wolves were in the bottom three at halfway and finished there, with Leicester one place above them. The biggest fall was Everton's, from eleventh to seventeenth, the biggest climb Aston Villa's, from tenth to sixth.
caption: League position after each club's 19th game (left) and final position (right), all twenty clubs.
chart_encode: Slope chart, left axis = table position after each club’s 19th game, right axis = final position. One line per club, all twenty.
chart_highlight: Manchester United (1st → 3rd) in accent, Arsenal (2nd → 1st) in second; Everton (11th → 17th, the biggest fall) labelled in ink.
chart_annotate: Points at halfway: United 46, Arsenal 45, Chelsea 42. | Biggest climbs: Aston Villa 10th → 6th, Bolton 12th → 8th, Tottenham 18th → 14th.
chart_notes: The position at game 19 is each club's own 19th game, so clubs are compared at the same number of games.
design_notes: Twenty lines is the limit for a slope; keep the 17 context lines at 0.5pt muted and push labels to the outer margins. | Club names on both axes in Label style, positions in tabular numerals.

headline: The champions came through their group second
stat_label: Porto’s points in Group F, three behind Real Madrid
body: The group stage ended on 10 December with few surprises at the top. Real Madrid won Group F with 14 points and lost none of their six games; Manchester United, Juventus and Chelsea topped theirs. Porto finished second in Real Madrid's group, three points behind, after losing 3-1 to them at home in October, their only defeat of the whole competition. Monaco won Group C on 11 points, scoring 15, eight of them in one night. Deportivo went through from the same group only on head-to-head, level on points with PSV. Nobody looking at these eight tables picked out the finalists.
caption: Final tables of the eight groups. Clubs in ink went through to the round of 16; third place went to the UEFA Cup.
source_line: Source: engsoccerdata (jalapic); tie-breaks per UEFA 2003–04 rules.
chart_encode: Eight mini tables (A–H) in a 4 × 2 grid, four per page; each row = club, points bar, W-D-L in results colours.
chart_highlight: Porto in accent, Monaco in second. Rows that went on to the round of 16 in ink, third place (to the UEFA Cup) in muted, fourth in draw-grey.
chart_annotate: Group C: Deportivo and PSV level on 10, Deportivo through on head-to-head. | English clubs won groups B, E and G.
chart_notes: Group order follows 2003-04 UEFA rules (head-to-head first), computed in spreads.py.
design_notes: Eight tables in one visual, four per page, identical scales on the points bars. | Tables in Label style; the group letter in Deck.

headline: United took 2.27 points a game before Ferdinand's ban and 1.56 after it
stat_label: United’s points per game from 20 January, down from 2.27
body: Rio Ferdinand missed a drugs test on 22 September. In December the FA banned him for eight months, and the ban began on 20 January. Up to then Manchester United had taken 50 points from 22 league games, 2.27 a game, and conceded 15. From then on they took 25 from 16, 1.56 a game, and conceded 20. Ferdinand was not the only reason. Ruud van Nistelrooy scored 20 league goals but the side around him was changing, and Arsenal and Chelsea were simply better over the spring. But the line on this strip is where United's title defence turned into a race for third. They won the FA Cup in May instead.
caption: Manchester United's league results in order, with points per game before and after Rio Ferdinand's ban began on 20 January 2004.
source_line: Source: football-data.co.uk; ban date from contemporary reports.
chart_encode: United’s 38 league results as one strip, game by game, W ink / D draw-grey / L accent; a thin running points-per-game line above it.
chart_highlight: A vertical rule at 20 January, labelled “Ferdinand’s ban begins”; the two ppg values set in Stat beside each half.
chart_annotate: Before: 22 games, 50 points, 15 conceded. After: 16 games, 25 points, 20 conceded.
chart_notes: The split falls between game 22 (17 Jan, Wolves 1–0 United) and game 23.
design_notes: Strip cells sized so 38 fit the chart region width (x 3.75–12); the rule at the split in ink 0.5pt. | Don't colour the halves differently; the results colours already carry it.
check_before_print: Ban start date 20 January 2004 is from contemporary reports, not our data; events.csv only has the 19 December hearing. | Correlation, not cause — the body says so; keep it.

headline: United went into February top, a point ahead of Arsenal with a game more played
stat_label: Manchester United’s points after 23 games, 31 January
body: At the end of January, Manchester United were top of the league on 53 points from 23 games. Arsenal were a point behind with a game in hand and still had a nought in the defeats column after 22. Chelsea were six further back. It was the last time United would lead at the end of a month. Ferdinand's ban had begun eleven days earlier; Arsenal had signed José Antonio Reyes from Sevilla for £10.5m. Over the next four weeks Arsenal won all five of their league games and United took five points from four. By the end of February the gap was nine points, the other way round.
caption: Premier League table at 31 January 2004.
source_line: Source: football-data.co.uk; 3/1/0, ties on GD then GF.
chart_encode: The full table at 31 January, 20 rows, columns P W D L GF GA GD Pts.
chart_highlight: United’s row in accent, Arsenal’s in second; the zero in Arsenal's L column set in Stat weight.
chart_annotate: Arsenal: 22 played, 15–7–0. United: 23 played, 17–2–4.
chart_notes: The last month-end United led; by the end of February Arsenal were nine clear.
design_notes: Table on the right page full height; tabular numerals, rules only every five rows. | Bottom three rows in draw-grey.

headline: Six clubs led the table. After 1 February, only Arsenal did
stat_label: Times the lead changed hands, all before 1 February
body: In the first two weeks of the season Blackburn, Manchester City and Portsmouth all spent a night at the top of the Premier League. By the end of the season six clubs had led it, and the lead had changed hands twenty times. Arsenal and Chelsea swapped it through the autumn; Manchester United held it for most of December and January. On 1 February Arsenal beat Manchester City 2-1 at Highbury and went top again. Nobody else led for the rest of the season. From that day the story stopped being who would win the league and became whether Arsenal could finish it unbeaten.
caption: The club top of the Premier League after each matchday, 2003-04. Each cell is one match date.
source_line: Source: football-data.co.uk; standings by date, 3/1/0, ties on GD then GF.
chart_encode: A ribbon of the 97 match dates, 16 August → 15 May, each cell coloured by the club top of the table that night.
chart_highlight: Arsenal’s cells in accent, Chelsea’s in second, United’s in ink; Blackburn, Manchester City and Portsmouth (August only) in muted with labels.
chart_annotate: A rule at 1 February: “the last change at the top”. | Days at the top: Arsenal 215, Manchester United 30, Chelsea 19, Blackburn 7, Man City 1, Portsmouth 1.
chart_notes: Cells are match dates, not calendar days; the days-at-the-top counts are calendar days between match dates.
design_notes: Ribbon is one row of 97 cells across the chart region, 8–10mm tall; labels for the August leaders sit above the cells. | The calendar-days counts as a small Label-style key under the ribbon, ordered by days.

headline: February was the season's highest-scoring month; March was the home sides'
stat_label: Goals per game in February 2004
body: The 380 league games produced 1,012 goals, 2.66 a game, but the months were not alike. October was the tightest, at 2.22 a game. February was the loosest: 125 goals in 39 matches, 3.21 a game, including Tottenham 4 Leicester 4. March was the odd month for a different reason. Home sides won 22 of its 34 games, almost two in three, when across the season they won fewer than half. None of this explains a title or a relegation, but it is the texture of a season, the weeks when every game seemed to finish 3-2 and the weeks when nobody could win away.
caption: Goals per game (left) and share of games won by the home side (right), by month. September (30 games) and March (34) are small samples.
chart_encode: Left: goals per game by month, August → May (10 bars). Right: home-win share by month (10 bars), same months.
chart_highlight: February in accent on the left, March in accent on the right; other months muted.
chart_annotate: Season average 2.66 goals a game: a 0.5pt reference line across the left bars. | March: home sides won 22 of 34 (64.7%); the season average was 43.9%.
chart_notes: Months with fewer matches (September 30, March 34) swing more; say so in the caption.
design_notes: Two bar charts sharing one month axis across the gutter; same bar width both sides.

headline: English clubs won three of the eight groups. None reached the final
stat_label: Groups won by English clubs: Arsenal, Manchester United, Chelsea
body: Four English clubs entered the 2003-04 Champions League and three of them won their groups: Arsenal after losing 3-0 at home to Inter on the first night, Manchester United with five wins from six, Chelsea in their first season of Abramovich's money. Then the knockouts took them one at a time. Newcastle had already gone in August. On 9 March United went out to Porto, 3-2 on aggregate. On 6 April Chelsea won at Highbury and knocked out Arsenal, the side nobody in England could beat. On 5 May Monaco beat Chelsea in the semi-final. The final had no English club in it.
caption: Every Champions League game played by the four English clubs, aligned by stage, with the tie that ended each run.
chart_encode: Four results strips stacked, one per English club, every Champions League game in order (Newcastle 2, Manchester United 8, Arsenal 10, Chelsea 14), aligned on a shared stage axis (Q3, groups, R16, QF, SF).
chart_highlight: Results colours only; each strip ends with the club’s exit labelled (date, opponent, aggregate).
chart_annotate: Newcastle: out 19 Aug, Partizan, penalties. United: out 9 Mar, Porto, 3–2. Arsenal: out 6 Apr, Chelsea, 3–2. Chelsea: out 5 May, Monaco, 5–3.
chart_notes: Strips aligned by stage, not date, so the groups line up.

stat_label: Arsenal’s unbeaten start, reached on 28 March (1–1 v Manchester United)

headline: Henry scored 30 league goals from 23.9 expected, seven of them in eight April days
stat_label: League goals, from 194 shots worth 23.9 xG
body: Thierry Henry took 194 league shots in 2003-04, worth 23.9 expected goals by StatsBomb's model, and scored 30. Seven were penalties and three free kicks; twenty came from open play. No one else in the league scored more than Alan Shearer's 22. Henry's April was the season in miniature. On Good Friday, 9 April, Liverpool led twice at Highbury and he scored a hat-trick; a week later he scored four against Leeds. Seven goals in eight days, as Arsenal came out of a fortnight in which they had gone out of the FA Cup and the Champions League. He was voted the footballer of the year by players and writers.
caption: Every league shot by Thierry Henry in 2003-04. Dot size is the chance's expected-goals value; filled dots are goals; ringed dots came in April.
source_line: Source: StatsBomb open data (Arsenal 2003/04); goals cross-checked with Wikipedia. StatsBomb logo and credit required.
chart_encode: Half-pitch shot map (StatsBomb 120 × 80, attacking right), every Henry league shot; dot area = xG, filled = goal, open = no goal.
chart_highlight: Goals filled in accent; the seven April goals (3 v Liverpool 9 Apr, 4 v Leeds 16 Apr) ringed in second.
chart_annotate: 7 penalties, 3 direct free kicks, 20 from open play. | Next best in the league: Shearer 22, Saha and Van Nistelrooy 20.
chart_notes: Coordinates are from the shooting team’s view; flip nothing.
design_notes: Pitch in rule colour on paper, half-pitch only, across the chart region; dot area ∝ xG with a three-dot size key in Label style. | StatsBomb logo bottom right of the chart region, per their licence.
check_before_print: Arsenal's FA Cup semi-final defeat (3 Apr, Manchester United) is not in our data; the Champions League exit (6 Apr) is.

headline: Two quarter-finals turned round in the second leg, and the holders went out
stat_label: Deportivo v Milan, 7 April, after losing 4–1 in Milan
body: Milan, the holders, won the first leg of their quarter-final 4-1 against Deportivo at San Siro, and Real Madrid beat Monaco 4-2 in Madrid. Both ties were thought settled. On 6 April Monaco won 3-1 at home and went through on away goals, Fernando Morientes, on loan from Real Madrid, scoring against the club that owned him. The next night Deportivo beat Milan 4-0 at the Riazor. The other two ties went the way the first legs pointed: Porto past Lyon, Chelsea past Arsenal. None of the four semi-finalists had won the Champions League; only Porto had won the European Cup, in 1987, before it took the name.
caption: Aggregate goal difference after each leg of the four quarter-finals, from the winners' side. Above zero, through.

chart_highlight: Deportivo in accent, Monaco in second; Porto and Chelsea in muted.

headline: Monaco had the competition’s two top scorers
stat_label: Champions League goals by Morientes (9) and Pršo (7)
body: Monaco did not only beat Real Madrid; they outscored everyone. Fernando Morientes finished the competition with nine goals in 1,026 minutes, Dado Pršo with seven in 512, the best rate of any regular scorer. Behind them came Roy Makaay of Bayern and Walter Pandiani of Deportivo on six. Thierry Henry, who scored 30 in the league, managed five in Europe, one every 178 minutes. Porto, the champions, had no one in the top eight: Benni McCarthy's four were their best. The champions' goals came from everywhere, the finalists' from two men.

headline: Twenty-six wins, twelve draws, and no defeats
stat_label: League defeats, Arsenal 2003–04
body: Arsenal finished the 2003-04 league season with 26 wins, 12 draws and no defeats, 73 goals scored and 26 conceded. They were behind at half-time five times and took 13 points from those games. They went to Old Trafford, Anfield and Stamford Bridge as the bookmakers' underdogs and lost none of the three. Their expected goals, by StatsBomb's model, came to 60.9 for and 30.9 against, a side that made twice the chances it allowed. The last game, 2-1 against Leicester on 15 May, came from a goal down. The next day more than 250,000 people lined the streets of Islington for the parade.

source_line: Source: football-data.co.uk results and odds; StatsBomb open data (xG). StatsBomb logo and credit required.

headline: Three clubs went down on 33 points. Everton stayed up on 39
stat_label: Points for Leicester, Leeds and Wolves, all relegated
body: Leicester, Leeds and Wolverhampton Wanderers all finished on 33 points and all went down. Leicester and Wolves had been promoted the summer before; Leeds, a Champions League semi-finalist three years earlier, were sinking under debt, sacked Peter Reid in November and conceded 79 goals, the most in the league. Wolves did not win a single away game. Leicester drew fifteen times, more than anyone except Newcastle. Above them, Everton slid from eleventh at halfway to seventeenth and survived on 39, six clear; Manchester City, top for one night in August, finished sixteenth. Portsmouth, the third promoted club, stayed up in thirteenth.

headline: Porto won the final 3–0 with four shots
stat_label: Porto’s expected goals in the final; Monaco had 0.68
body: Neither club in the final at the Arena AufSchalke on 26 May had been anyone's favourite in August, and the game was as lopsided in the score as it was even on the pitch. Monaco had more of the ball, 511 passes to 427, and more of the shots, nine to four. Porto scored with three of theirs. Carlos Alberto scored just before half-time; Deco and Dmitri Alenichev added two more in four minutes midway through the second half. By StatsBomb's model the three chances were worth half a goal between them. José Mourinho's side had won the UEFA Cup a year earlier. A week later he was Chelsea's manager.
caption: Every shot in the 2004 Champions League final. Dot size is the chance's expected-goals value; filled dots are goals.

headline: Porto lost once in thirteen games. Monaco lost four times and still got there
stat_label: Porto’s defeats in the competition: 1–3 v Real Madrid, 1 October
body: The two finalists took different roads to Gelsenkirchen. Porto played thirteen games and lost one, at home to Real Madrid in October; they drew five, including both legs that mattered most, 1-1 at Old Trafford and 2-2 in Lyon. They scored 20 and conceded 12. Monaco lost four times, at Deportivo, in Moscow, in Madrid and in the final itself, and scored 27, more than anyone. They went through two knockout ties on away goals. Porto's road was the steadier one, and the final went the steady side's way.

kicker: Season in numbers · Against the odds
headline: Arsenal beat the bookmakers' prices by fourteen points
stat_label: Arsenal’s points above what Bet365’s odds implied
body: Bookmakers set a price on every game, and the prices add up to a forecast. Take the margin out of Bet365's odds for each of Arsenal's 38 games and they implied about 76 points; Arsenal took 90. Bolton, under Sam Allardyce, beat their prices by almost nine. At the other end Manchester City, Leeds and Everton each fell about ten points short of what the market expected of them. The biggest single upset by the odds was Middlesbrough's 3-2 win at Old Trafford in February, a result the prices gave less than a one-in-eleven chance.

source_line: Source: football-data.co.uk (Bet365 odds), margin removed by normalising the three implied probabilities.

headline: Portugal sent two clubs. One of them won it
stat_label: Countries with a club in the 2003–04 Champions League
body: Forty-eight countries had a club in the 2003-04 Champions League, from the Faroe Islands to Russia. Portugal sent two. Benfica went out in the last qualifying round in August; Porto won the whole thing. England, Spain and Italy sent four each and Germany three; between them they supplied two of the four semi-finalists and neither finalist. France reached the final through Monaco. Most of the table is the long tail of Europe's smaller leagues, whose champions played two or three ties in July and August and were gone before the group stage began.

headline: Eight of the fifteen knockout ties came down to one goal or away goals
stat_label: Knockout ties decided by one goal on aggregate or on away goals
body: The knockout rounds of 2003-04 were close. Of the fifteen ties from the round of 16 to the final, eight were settled by a single goal or on away goals. Monaco survived twice on away goals, against Lokomotiv Moscow and Real Madrid, and Porto went through two by one goal, Manchester United 3-2 and Deportivo 1-0, with Lyon 4-2 the comfortable one between. Only the final was a rout. Read the bracket from left to right and the big names leave it in order: Bayern and Juventus in March, Real Madrid, Milan and Arsenal in April, Chelsea in May.
